summary: This memo specifies two prime-order groups, ristretto255 and decaf448, for building cryptographic protocols safely. ristretto255 can be implemented on Curve25519, so existing implementations can be reused. decaf448 is similarly built on edwards448. It comes from the Crypto Forum Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: Many cryptographic protocols assume a group of points where every point except the identity is equally hard to attack. The fastest elliptic curves do not give that: their points split into a large group and several small ones, and each protocol has to handle the small ones in its own way, which is where subtle bugs come from. These two group definitions put that handling in one place, on top of the existing Curve25519 and edwards448 code.

subtitle: Safe prime-order elliptic curve groups for cryptographic protocols.

tldr.problem: Many group-based cryptographic protocols assume a group of prime order, where every element except the identity generates the whole group, but the fastest elliptic curves have a group order with a cofactor, and the usual workarounds are ad hoc and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: ristretto255 and decaf448 are abstract group interfaces built on Curve25519 and edwards448, using mathematical transformations to present a prime-order abstraction with validation built into decoding and canonical encodings.
tldr.outcome: Protocol implementors get the group they assumed, on top of fast curve implementations they already have, with the cofactor pitfalls handled in one place instead of in every protocol.

today: RFC 9496 is an Informational RFC published in December 2023 by the Crypto Forum Research Group. It has not been obsoleted and is the consensus specification of the two groups.

sections.title: The Problem With Cofactors
sections.content:
Decaf is a technique for constructing prime-order groups with nonmalleable encodings from non-prime-order elliptic curves. Ristretto extends this technique to support cofactor-8 curves such as Curve25519. In particular, this allows an existing Curve25519 library to provide a prime-order group with only a thin abstraction layer.

Many group-based cryptographic protocols require the number of elements in the group, the group order, to be prime. Prime-order groups are useful because every non-identity element of the group generates the entire group: the group has a cofactor of 1, and all elements are equivalent from the perspective of the hardness of the discrete logarithm problem.

Edwards curves provide a number of implementation benefits. The formulas for curve operations are among the fastest currently known, and the addition formulas are complete with no exceptional points. However, the group of points on the curve is not of prime order: it has a cofactor larger than 1. This abstraction mismatch is usually handled, if it is handled at all, by ad hoc protocol tweaks such as multiplying by the cofactor in an appropriate place.

Even for simple protocols such as signatures, these tweaks can cause subtle issues. Ed25519 implementations may have different validation behaviour between batched and singleton verification, and, at least as specified in RFC 8032, the set of valid signatures is not defined precisely. For more complex protocols, careful analysis is required, since the original security proofs may no longer apply, and the tweaks for one protocol may have disastrous effects when applied to another, as in the octuple-spend vulnerability in one-time ring signatures.

Decaf and Ristretto fix this abstraction mismatch in one place for all protocols, providing an abstraction to protocol implementors that matches the abstraction commonly assumed in protocol specifications while still allowing the use of high-performance curve implementations internally. The abstraction layer imposes minor overhead, and only in the encoding and decoding phases.

While Ristretto is a general method usable with any Edwards curve with cofactor 4 or 8, this document specifies the ristretto255 group, which can be implemented using Curve25519, and the decaf448 group, which can be implemented using edwards448. Other elliptic curves could be used internally to implement the same two groups, and those implementations would be interoperable with one based on Curve25519 or edwards448, but those constructions are out of scope. The document represents the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group; it is not an IETF product and not a standard.
sections.plainLanguage: A curve's points form a big group plus a few tiny ones. A protocol that assumes only the big group has to neutralise the tiny ones, usually by multiplying by a fixed number at some point in the arithmetic. Doing that by hand in every protocol is where mistakes happen, and the mistakes have been serious. This RFC moves that step into the group definition itself, once, for everyone.

sections.title: The Group Abstraction
sections.content:
Ristretto and Decaf implement an abstract prime-order group interface that exposes only the behaviour useful to higher-level protocols, without leaking curve-related details and pitfalls. Each abstract group exposes operations on abstract element and abstract scalar types: decoding, encoding, equality, addition, negation, subtraction and multi-scalar multiplication. Each group also exposes a deterministic function to derive abstract elements from fixed-length byte strings.

Decoding is a function from byte strings to abstract elements with built-in validation, so that only the canonical encodings of valid elements are accepted. The built-in validation removes the need for explicit invalid curve checks.

Encoding is a function from abstract elements to byte strings. Internally an abstract element may have more than one possible representation, for example in projective coordinates, but all equivalent representations of the same element encode as identical byte strings, and decoding the output of the encoding function always succeeds and returns an element equivalent to the encoding input.

The equality check reports whether two representations of an abstract element are equivalent. The element derivation function maps deterministically from byte strings of a fixed length to abstract elements. It has two important properties. First, if the input is a uniformly random byte string, the output is, within a negligible statistical distance, a uniformly random abstract group element, which makes it suitable for selecting random group elements. Second, although the function is many-to-one and therefore not strictly invertible, it is not pre-image resistant: given an arbitrary abstract group element there is an efficient algorithm to randomly sample from the byte strings that map to it. In some contexts that would be a weakness, but it matters in others: it means a combination of a cryptographic hash function and the element derivation function is suitable to define encoding functions such as hash_to_ristretto255 and hash_to_decaf448.

Addition is the group operation. The group has an identity element and prime order l; adding l copies of the same element gives the identity, and adding the identity to any element returns that element unchanged. Negation returns an element that, added to its input, gives the identity. Subtraction is the addition of a negated element, and scalar multiplication is the repeated addition of an element.
sections.plainLanguage: The interface a protocol sees has eight operations: turn bytes into an element, turn an element into bytes, compare two elements, add, subtract, negate, multiply by a number, and derive an element from a fixed-length string. Decoding validates as it goes, so the caller never has to check whether a point is on the curve. Encoding is canonical, so the same element always produces the same bytes.

sections.title: ristretto255 Elements and Scalars
sections.content:
ristretto255 is an instantiation of the abstract prime-order group interface, implemented using Curve25519 points as internal representations. A ristretto255 group element is the abstract element of the prime-order group, an element encoding is the unique reversible encoding of a group element, and an internal representation is a point on the curve used to implement ristretto255. Each group element can have multiple equivalent internal representations. Encoding, decoding, equality and the element derivation function are defined here; element addition, subtraction, negation and scalar multiplication are implemented by applying the corresponding operations directly to the internal representation.

The group order is the same as the order of the Curve25519 prime-order subgroup: 2^252 plus 27742317777372353535851937790883648493. Because ristretto255 is a prime-order group, every element except the identity is a generator. For interoperability a canonical generator is selected, which can be internally represented by the Curve25519 base point, enabling reuse of existing precomputation for scalar multiplication. Its encoding is the 32-byte string beginning e2f2ae0a.

All elements are encoded as 32-byte strings. Decoding interprets the string as an unsigned integer in little-endian representation; if the length is not 32 bytes, or the value is greater than or equal to the field prime p, decoding fails. Unlike the field element decoding of RFC 7748, the most significant bit is not masked and non-canonical values are rejected. If IS_NEGATIVE(s) returns TRUE, decoding fails. The remaining steps compute a field element u1 from 1 minus s squared and u2 from 1 plus s squared, obtain an inverse square root of a ratio of field elements, and form the internal representation (x, y, 1, t). If the square root was not a square, or IS_NEGATIVE(t) is TRUE, or y is zero, decoding fails; otherwise the element is returned.

Encoding processes the internal representation into a field element s, using an inverse square root and a conditional rotation of x and y, and returns the 32-byte little-endian encoding of s as an integer between 0 and p-1 inclusive. Decoding and then re-encoding a valid group element yields an identical byte string.

The equality function returns TRUE when two internal representations correspond to the same group element, and internal representations MUST NOT be compared in any other way. It always returns TRUE when applied to an internal representation and to the representation obtained by encoding and then re-decoding it, although those representations might not be identical. Implementations MAY also perform constant-time byte comparisons on the encodings for an equivalent, less efficient result.

The element derivation function operates on 64-byte strings, obtained from an arbitrary-length string with a domain-separated hash construction whose choice is out of scope. It computes P1 as MAP of the first 32 bytes and P2 as MAP of the last 32 bytes, and returns P1 plus P2. The MAP function masks the most significant bit of the final byte, interprets the string as a little-endian unsigned integer and reduces it modulo p to a field element t; unlike decoding, the most significant bit is masked here and non-canonical values are accepted.

The scalars for the group are integers modulo the group order, the same scalar field as Curve25519, so existing implementations can be reused. Scalars are encoded as 32-byte strings in little-endian order. Implementations SHOULD check that a scalar falls in the range from 0 up to but not including the group order when parsing, and reject non-canonical encodings, and SHOULD reduce scalars modulo the order when encoding them. Omitting these strict range checks is NOT RECOMMENDED but is allowed so that existing scalar arithmetic implementations can be reused. From a uniformly distributed 64-byte string, a uniformly distributed scalar is obtained by interpreting it as a 512-bit little-endian unsigned integer and reducing it modulo the order.
sections.plainLanguage: The 25519 version encodes every element in 32 bytes. Decoding refuses anything that is not a canonical, non-negative representation, so a caller cannot feed in a point that lies outside the group. The order of the group is the prime the curve's subgroup has, and the scalar arithmetic is the same as Curve25519's, so the code underneath can be reused as it is.

sections.title: decaf448 Elements, Scalars and the Shared Helper
sections.content:
decaf448 is the second instantiation of the abstract prime-order group interface, implemented using edwards448 points as internal representations. Its group order is the same as the order of the edwards448 prime-order subgroup: 2^446 minus 13818066809895115352007386748515426880336692474882178609894547503885. As with ristretto255, every element except the identity is a generator, and a canonical generator is selected for interoperability, internally represented by twice the edwards448 base point so that existing precomputation can be reused. Its encoding is the repeating pattern of 66666666 and 33333333 bytes, which equals 1 over the square root of 5 in the field and corresponds to the curve448 base point with x equal to 5.

All decaf448 elements are encoded as 56-byte strings. Decoding interprets the string as an unsigned integer in little-endian representation and fails if the length is not 56 bytes or the value is greater than or equal to the field prime; unlike the field element decoding of RFC 7748, non-canonical values are rejected. It then computes the internal representation and fails if the square root was not a square. Encoding produces the 56-byte little-endian encoding of the canonical representation of the field element s.

The element derivation function operates on 112-byte strings, computing P1 as MAP of the first 56 bytes and P2 as MAP of the last 56 bytes and returning their sum. The MAP function interprets the string as a little-endian unsigned integer and reduces it modulo p, accepting non-canonical values. The scalars for decaf448 are integers modulo the group order, the same scalar field as edwards448, and are encoded as 56-byte strings in little-endian order, with the same recommendation to check the range and reject non-canonical encodings.

Both groups share a helper for taking the square root of a ratio of field elements. Given u and v, the function SQRT_RATIO_M1 returns the nonnegative square root of u divided by v together with a flag saying whether the ratio was a square; it returns a zero with TRUE when u is zero, a zero with FALSE when v is zero and u is not, and, when the ratio is not a square, a square root of the ratio multiplied by a fixed constant with FALSE. The computation is similar to that in RFC 8032, with the difference that a non-square input produces a result with a defined relationship to the inputs, which is what makes the derivation function efficient. The function can be refactored from an existing Ed25519 or edwards448 implementation.

Several operations are assumed to be implemented in constant time, so that the time taken does not depend on secret values: a constant-time equality, a constant-time select that returns one of two values depending on a condition, and a constant-time absolute value that returns the negation of a value when it is negative. The document defines IS_NEGATIVE to be TRUE when the least nonnegative integer representing a field element is odd, and recommends it be implemented in constant time.
sections.plainLanguage: The 448-bit version works the same way with larger numbers: 56-byte elements, a 112-byte input to the derivation function, and the same scalar arithmetic as edwards448. Both groups need a helper that takes a square root of a ratio of field elements, which returns an answer whether or not the ratio is a square, and that helper can be lifted straight out of an existing Ed25519 implementation.

sections.title: API and Security Considerations
sections.content:
ristretto255 and decaf448 are abstractions that implement two prime-order groups. Their elements are represented by curve points but are not curve points, and implementations SHOULD reflect that fact: the type representing an element SHOULD be opaque to the caller, not exposing the underlying curve point or field elements, and implementations SHOULD NOT expose internal constants or functions used in implementing the group operations.

The reason for this encapsulation is that ristretto255 and decaf448 implementations can change their underlying curve without causing a breaking change. The constructions are carefully designed so that this will be the case, as long as implementations do not expose internal representations or operate on them except as described in the document. In particular, implementations SHOULD NOT define any external interface as operating on arbitrary curve points, and SHOULD NOT construct group elements except via decoding, the element derivation function, or group operations on other valid group elements. They may apply any optimization strategy to the internal representations as long as it does not change the exposed behaviour of the API. It is also RECOMMENDED that implementations not perform a decoding and encoding operation for each group operation, since that is inefficient and unnecessary; implementations SHOULD instead provide an opaque type to hold the internal representation across multiple operations.

On security, the two groups give higher-level protocols the abstraction they expect, a prime-order group, so it is expected to be safer in any situation where Curve25519 or edwards448 is used to implement a protocol requiring a prime-order group. The safety of the abstraction can be defeated by implementations that do not follow the API guidance. There is no function to test whether an elliptic curve point is a valid internal representation of a group element: the decoding function always returns a valid internal representation or an error, and the operations exposed by the group return valid internal representations when applied to valid ones. An implementation can therefore maintain the invariant that an internal representation is always valid, so that checking is never necessary and invalid states are unrepresentable.
sections.plainLanguage: The implementation advice is about discipline. If the API hands out the underlying curve point, a caller can construct invalid elements and break the very guarantee the group provides, and future versions lose the freedom to change the curve underneath. Keep the element type opaque, keep the operations on it, and invalid states cannot be represented at all.

viz.caption: THE ABSTRACTION MISMATCH THESE GROUPS FIX

cells: Not prime, with a cofactor larger than 1
Every element except the identity generates the whole group
Small subgroups exist, and their elements behave differently
Ad hoc tweaks, such as multiplying by the cofactor in an appropriate place
Subtle validation differences between implementations, and proofs that no longer apply

viz.caption: THE OPERATIONS THE GROUP INTERFACE EXPOSES

items.label: Decode
items.desc: Turns a byte string into an element, accepting only the canonical encodings of valid elements.

items.label: Encode
items.desc: Turns an element into a byte string; equivalent representations always give identical bytes.

items.label: Equals
items.desc: Reports whether two representations are the same element.

items.label: Addition
items.desc: The group operation, with an identity element and prime order.

items.label: Negation
items.desc: Returns the element that added to its input gives the identity.

items.label: Element derivation
items.desc: Maps a fixed-length byte string deterministically to an element.
